subject: design-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the Edexcel GCSE Design & Technology specification, what is a 'design context'?
options: A situation or setting that provides the starting point for design opportunities and needs
A finished manufacturing specification for a product
A list of the exact materials a product must be made from
A legal contract between a designer and a manufacturer
questions.explain: A design context is the situation or environment from which a designer identifies problems, needs and opportunities to explore.

questions.q: Why does a designer investigate a design context before generating ideas?
options: To identify the needs and wants of users and stakeholders within that situation
To decide the retail price before any research is carried out
To avoid having to produce any prototypes
To guarantee the product will win a design award
questions.explain: Exploring the context reveals the genuine needs, wants and problems of users so that design outcomes are relevant.

questions.q: A brief gives the context 'reducing food waste in the home'. Which is the most appropriate design opportunity from this context?
options: A storage system that keeps fresh produce usable for longer
A faster petrol engine for a delivery van
A brighter packaging colour for a chocolate bar
A cheaper way to print restaurant menus
questions.explain: The opportunity must directly address the stated context of reducing food waste in the home.

questions.q: Who are 'stakeholders' when investigating a design context?
options: People or groups affected by, or with an interest in, the product or design decision
Only the designer who creates the product
The machines used to manufacture the product
The retailers who sell competing brands
questions.explain: Stakeholders are the individuals and groups who have an interest in or are affected by the product, such as users, clients and manufacturers.

questions.q: Which set correctly lists the '6 Rs' used to assess the sustainability of a product?
options: Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repair, Recycle
Recycle, Reheat, Reduce, Reuse, Remake, Return
Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Rewind, Reset, Repair
Rethink, Reduce, Restore, Reuse, Remove, Recycle
questions.explain: The 6 Rs are Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repair and Recycle.

questions.q: Which action best represents the 'Reduce' principle of the 6 Rs?
options: Using less material or energy to make and run a product
Buying a completely different type of product instead
Melting waste plastic down to form new products
Returning a broken product to the manufacturer
questions.explain: 'Reduce' means minimising the material, energy and waste associated with a product.

questions.q: A resource such as oil or coal that cannot be replaced within a human lifetime is described as:
options: Finite (non-renewable)
Infinite (renewable)
Biodegradable
Recyclable by default
questions.explain: Fossil fuels like oil and coal are finite (non-renewable) because they take millions of years to form and will eventually run out.

questions.q: Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?
options: Wind
Coal
Natural gas
Crude oil
questions.explain: Wind is a renewable energy source because it is naturally replenished and does not run out.

questions.q: What does a product's 'carbon footprint' measure?
options: The total greenhouse gas emissions associated with the product
The weight of the product in kilograms
The number of parts inside the product
The distance a customer travels to buy the product
questions.explain: A carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gases produced across a product's life, usually expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent.

questions.q: What is a life cycle assessment (LCA) of a product?
options: An evaluation of a product's environmental impact from raw material extraction to disposal
A test of how long the product will keep working
A calculation of the product's retail profit margin
A survey of how much customers like the product
questions.explain: An LCA assesses environmental impact across the whole life of a product, from material extraction through manufacture, use and disposal.

questions.q: Why do designers try to reduce the number of 'product miles' (transport distance) for a product?
options: To lower the fuel used in transport and reduce emissions
To make the product physically heavier
To increase the amount of packaging used
To slow down how quickly the product reaches shops
questions.explain: Fewer product miles means less fuel is burned moving materials and goods, reducing pollution and carbon emissions.

questions.q: A company wants to make its packaging more sustainable. Which change best applies the 6 Rs?
options: Redesigning it to use less card and to be recyclable
Adding an extra layer of non-recyclable plastic film
Making it larger so it looks more attractive
Printing it with more colours of ink
questions.explain: Using less material (Reduce) and making it recyclable (Recycle) directly applies the 6 Rs to lower environmental impact.

questions.q: A material that can be broken down naturally by microorganisms is described as:
options: Biodegradable
Thermosetting
Non-ferrous
Composite
questions.explain: Biodegradable materials can be decomposed by microorganisms, reducing long-term waste in landfill.

questions.q: What does the 'Fairtrade' mark indicate about a product?
options: Producers in developing countries received a fair, guaranteed price for their goods
The product is the cheapest option available
The product is made entirely from recycled materials
The product was manufactured within the UK
questions.explain: The Fairtrade mark shows that producers were paid a fair and stable price and worked under agreed social and environmental standards.

Designing a product to last as long as possible
Recycling a product at the end of its life
Repairing a product free of charge for the customer
questions.explain: Planned obsolescence is designing products to become outdated or fail so consumers buy replacements, which raises social and environmental concerns.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a social challenge a designer should consider?
options: Making sure a product is inclusive and accessible to a range of users
Choosing the largest possible profit margin only
Selecting the fastest available machine tool
Maximising the number of colours in the packaging
questions.explain: Considering inclusivity and accessibility addresses the social needs of diverse users, including those with disabilities.

questions.q: What does 'ethical sourcing' of materials mean?
options: Obtaining materials in ways that are fair to workers and considerate of the environment
Buying materials only from the nearest supplier
Choosing materials purely on the lowest price
Using only materials that are coloured naturally
questions.explain: Ethical sourcing means materials are obtained with fair treatment of workers and reduced harm to the environment.

questions.q: The impact of manufacturing that moves production to countries with cheaper labour is an example of which type of challenge?
options: Economic and social
Purely aesthetic
Purely mechanical
Purely electronic
questions.explain: Global manufacturing decisions affect jobs, wages and communities, making them economic and social challenges.

questions.q: A designer must choose a supplier for a wooden toy. Which choice best addresses environmental and social responsibility?
options: A supplier using FSC-certified timber and fair working conditions
The supplier offering the lowest price regardless of source
A supplier using timber from unregulated logging
A supplier that ships the wood the longest distance
questions.explain: FSC certification ensures timber comes from responsibly managed forests, and fair working conditions address social responsibility.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Design & Technology (1DT0) specification; Contexts, Environmental, Social & Economic Challenges
